justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish baseline assumption across all three horizons. For the one-day estimate around 195.5, I was largely anchoring to recent price action and momentum, assuming no major overnight catalysts would materially shift the market. The slight upward drift to 197 at one week and 200 at one month reflects a modest positive drift assumption consistent with long-run equity market tendencies, as well as mean-reversion dynamics if recent prices were slightly depressed relative to fair value. These estimates essentially embed a view that the underlying asset — likely a broad equity index or individual stock — continues along a gradual upward trajectory absent significant shocks.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the well-established principle that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% confidence interval spans roughly 15 points, which is consistent with typical daily volatility in equity markets. At one week, that range expands to 30 points, and at one month it widens to 64 points. These widths were calibrated using implied or historical volatility estimates, scaled appropriately by the square root of time. I also widened the intervals somewhat beyond a pure statistical approach to account for fat tails — real financial returns are not normally distributed and extreme events occur more frequently than a Gaussian model would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals in either direction. On the downside, a sudden macroeconomic shock — such as an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant earnings disappointment — could easily breach the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. Credit events or liquidity crises have historically caused drawdowns far exceeding what standard volatility models would predict. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst such as a ceasefire in an ongoing conflict, a dovish policy pivot, or a blowout earnings report could drive prices beyond the upper bound. Structural breaks in the volatility regime — for instance, a transition from a low-volatility environment to a high-volatility one — would also render these intervals too narrow in retrospect.
